analysis.one_liner: Orders federal regulators to crack down on excessive speculation that drives up oil and gasoline prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 21 senators behind it, was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the agency that polices futures markets — to use its emergency powers within 14 days to curb excessive speculation in energy futures and swaps, and to eliminate price distortions it was causing. The bill's findings argue that speculation was pushing gasoline prices far above what supply and demand justified, costing drivers at the pump. It was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and anyone who pays for heating fuel, shipping, or airfare — all of whom bear the cost when energy prices are pushed above what supply and demand justify. The bill's findings cite an estimate that speculation added roughly 56 cents to a gallon of gasoline [S3]; curbing it would put that money back in consumers' pockets. Commercial fuel buyers like airlines, which hedge with futures, would also benefit from less price distortion [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and anyone who buys fuel

how_it_helps.text: It orders the CFTC, within 14 days, to curb excessive speculation in energy futures and swaps and to eliminate price distortions that keep markets from tracking real supply and demand.

The bill's findings point to a real-world cost for drivers: in June 2014, gasoline supply was higher and demand lower than in 2009, yet the average price was over $3.68 a gallon versus $2.64 then — a gap the bill attributes to speculation, which it says added roughly 56 cents per gallon according to a Goldman Sachs estimate.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms — banks, hedge funds, and index funds — that profit from large speculative positions in oil and gasoline futures and swaps. If speculation genuinely inflates prices, the cost they bear would be a transfer of savings to consumers, but legitimate hedgers could also face higher costs for locking in fuel prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's premise rests on contested economics: it cites a Goldman Sachs estimate that speculation added about 56 cents to a gallon of gasoline, but other analysts attribute most price movements to supply and demand, so the actual savings could be far smaller than the findings imply.

The bill orders the CFTC to act within 14 days of enactment, regardless of market conditions; blunt, automatic intervention in futures markets could also disrupt legitimate hedging by airlines, trucking firms, and utilities that buy energy contracts to lock in costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculation really adds tens of cents to a gallon of gas, the consumer benefit would be large and the cost to the public small, since legitimate hedging by airlines and fuel buyers would still be allowed. The honest caveat is that the link between speculation and pump prices is disputed, so the guaranteed gains are smaller than the bill's findings suggest; and the hard 14-day deadline, written before anyone studied the market at that moment, is blunt by design. On balance a modest, well-targeted consumer protection that was never allowed a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry — the committee with jurisdiction over commodity futures regulation.
The complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever taken after the referral.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired with it, having never come to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that speculate in energy futures keep operating without new position limits, and gasoline consumers never got the price relief the bill aimed for. The committee that declined to act faced no recorded consequence.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks arguing excessive speculation was inflating gasoline prices.

for.name: 20 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sherrod Brown, Elizabeth Warren, Ed Markey, and Amy Klobuchar

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over commodity futures regulation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 26, 2014 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all 21 supporters were Democrats or the independent Sanders, so partisan alignment can be inferred for sponsors but not for any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Energy futures speculators (banks, hedge funds, and index traders)
industries.note: The bill directs regulators to curb and eliminate excessive speculative positions in energy futures and swaps, directly limiting this trading activity and its profits. Ordinary consumers pay the speculation premium at the pump, so the industry's interest runs against theirs.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Speculation-driven price premiums raise revenues when prices are high, but volatility also distorts planning. The bill targets the trading around oil, not oil production itself.
These firms use energy futures to lock in fuel costs, and aggressive position limits could raise their hedging costs — though lower, less volatile pump prices would ultimately help them too.
